title: They Took His Pulpit. Not His Words.
hook: They took his pulpit and sent him to jail. *He kept preaching anyway.*
dateline: Joseph Alleine · Died on this day, November 17, 1668 · Bath, England
summary: On November 17, 1668, Joseph Alleine died at 34, silenced and jailed for preaching. His Alarm to the Unconverted is still in print.

story: He had made one request about his body: if he died within fifty miles of Taunton, he wanted to be carried back and buried there. On November 17, 1668, 358 years ago today, Joseph Alleine died in Bath, worn out at 34. They brought him home and laid him in the chancel of St Mary Magdalene, the church he had been barred from preaching in.

He had come to Taunton, in Somerset, in 1655, as assistant to its minister, George Newton. That October he married Theodosia Alleine, daughter of the minister Richard Alleine. She ran a boarding school in their home. Five afternoons a week he went house to house, talking with families about God. His wife later wrote that her only complaint was that he was so busy she "could have but very little converse with him."

Then, in 1662, a new law, the Act of Uniformity, required every minister to conform to the Church of England's prayer book. About 2,000 refused and lost their pulpits. Alleine was one of them. He was 28.

He didn't stop. He kept preaching wherever he could. One Saturday evening in May 1663 he was arrested, and he spent nearly a year in the jail at Ilchester, writing letters to his people in Taunton. Released on May 26, 1664, he went straight back to preaching, and was jailed again. His health broke under it.
Not everyone admired him. A hostile contemporary, the Oxford historian Anthony Wood, called his life "busie, forward" and meddling. But even that complaint describes a man who couldn't stop.

Alleine wrote with the same urgency. His *Alarm to Unconverted Sinners* was printed after his death, in 1671 or 1672; sources disagree. It is blunt, even fierce. But read closely, it is begging. He wanted to "weep out every argument," he wrote, and "empty my veins for ink."

People read it. The *Dictionary of National Biography* reports 20,000 copies sold on its first appearance, and 50,000 more when it was reissued as *A Sure Guide to Heaven*. Methodist preaching-houses later sold it. And as a boy under conviction of sin, Charles Spurgeon reached for it, or Baxter's *Call*, first thing in the morning.
A law had taken his pulpit. It couldn't take the words. They are still in print.

why: Joseph Alleine was silenced at 28 and dead at 34. His *Alarm to Unconverted Sinners* is still in print, more than 350 years later, as *A Sure Guide to Heaven*. A law took his pulpit. It couldn't take what God had given him to say, and it still reaches people who never saw Taunton.
